doc_summary: A position paper arguing that adversarial ML for LLMs studies problems that are harder to define, solve, and evaluate than classical adversarial robustness, so progress is hard to track; it recommends explicit goals and well-scoped formal sub-problems. It includes a notable discussion of what a rigorous, realistic agent environment requires and why LLM judges and simulated environments weaken evidence.

items.claim: Prefers a realistic, fully scaffolded agent environment with tool use over simplified simulated environments judged by LLMs, because rigorous measurement of attack success needs real-world-like interaction.
items.quote: Rigor ously evaluating the effectiveness of prompt injection attacks and defenses necessitates a realistic AI agent environment that closely mimics real-world scenarios. Such an environment should include comprehensive system scaffolding with tool use, enabling the simulation of complex interactions.

items.claim: Distrusts evaluations that simulate environments for simplicity and rely on LLM judges, since they trade rigor for convenience and make outcomes less precisely measurable.
items.quote: However, for simplicity, many studies opt to simulate these environments and rely on LLMs as judges for evaluation. There are new setups that have more rigorous evaluations (Debenedetti et al., 2024), where the attack's success and utility can be precisely measured

items.claim: Prefers outcomes that can be directly and objectively measured (e.g., an unauthorized action actually taken) over subjective judgments of text, because clear success criteria make evidence convincing.
items.quote: The primary goal of prompt injections is often clear— for instance, manipulating a language model to perform unauthorized actions like sending emails (Debenedetti et al., 2024), where success can be directly measured.

items.claim: Distrusts LLM-as-judge scoring because judges diverge from humans, can be fooled, and create circular correlations with the system under test.
items.quote: First, such judges still fall short of human judgment. For instance, many implementations of ten default to considering any non-refusal response as a successful attack even if the content is harmless

items.claim: Rejects trivial or non-novel elicitations as evidence of a real vulnerability; a valid test must reveal something meaningfully new rather than just echoing the request.
items.quote: trivial attacks such as prompting "please repeat [harmful text]" do not reveal meaningful new vulnerabilities. Hence, there is no clear universal standard on what sorts of prompts or transformations count as "valid" or "novel" adversarial inputs.

items.claim: Distrusts reported progress and defense evaluations that are not adaptive or worst-case, since original evaluations often overestimate robustness and average-case gains hide worst-case failures.
items.quote: we must distinguish between progress in preventing average-case vulnerabilities and achieving worst-case security robustness. Although we might be making progress in the former, we have barely improved the latter and most models can still produce harmful generations under attacks.

items.claim: Prefers manual, context-dependent, human-style attacks (persona, multi-turn, social engineering) over automated optimization for finding worst cases, because they are what actually works on LLMs.
items.quote: Many successful attacks on LLMs exploit qualitative properties that are hard to optimize automatically, such as persona modulation (Shah et al., 2023), multi-turn conver sations (Anil et al., 2024), and social engineering techniques (Zeng et al., 2024).

items.claim: Prefers papers that state explicitly whether they pursue real-world security demonstration or scientific understanding, and are judged accordingly, because the two purposes warrant different standards of rigor.
items.quote: Papers should be explicit for what reason they are being written, and should be evaluated in this light. For real-world security, demonstrating attacks on fuzzy, ill-defined problems can be valuable when the potential harm is clear and immediate.

items.claim: Distrusts results on closed, silently updated systems because the tested version is unclear and findings cannot be reproduced or compared.
items.quote: Many influential LLMs are now closed-source and updated silently over time (Chao et al., 2024), making it unclear which version of a system is being tested.

items.claim: Prefers carefully scoped, formal, well-defined sub-problems over attacking the whole fuzzy space without rigor, because only these let progress be measured and built upon.
items.quote: Attempting to solve the entire space of attacks without rigor is neither scientific nor likely to be productive.
